1.0 is the claim that the shape survived contact with a SECOND implementation.
DemoViewer.NET implemented the contract over its own EntityState/EntityTracker
runtime against 0.1.1 and reported no contract change required, no runtime
hooks added, 43 conformance tests passing (SDK#6). On 0.1.1 the criterion is
met.
But this release is not 0.1.1. Their findings changed the reference reader --
TryReadEntityHandle now folds integral widths rather than converting them --
and added normative wording about cross-shape Vector3/QAngle reads. They
validated the reader BEFORE those changes, and their conformance port encodes
the old behaviour. Declaring 1.0 on code the second implementation has not run
would assert exactly the thing the criterion exists to establish, on evidence
that does not cover it.
So: 0.2 now, re-validation next, 1.0 when they confirm against this reader.
0.2 rather than another 0.1.x for two independent reasons, either sufficient.
In 0.x the minor is the breaking slot, and TryReadEntityHandle changing from a
checked conversion to an unchecked fold is a behaviour change a consumer can
observe -- a handle that used to read absent now reads as the invalid sentinel.
And mechanically, editing this file restarts the git height, so holding at 0.1
would have resolved 0.1.0 -- BELOW the published 0.1.1, leaving the feed
serving the older package as newest forever. That is the trap
CS2OpenDev.Sdk.GameEvents' versionHeightOffset was created to escape; a minor
bump clears it without the offset.
It does NOT track the family major. Sdk, Sdk.GameEvents and Protos share a
major because they are one product regenerated together; this is a contract
with its own life, and pinning it to the schema's major would mean a Valve
patch could bump the version of a file nobody touched. The family went 4.1 ->
5.0 while this sat at 0.1.1, which is the arrangement working.
// versionHeightOffset: Cancels the commit that changes `version` above, so a MAJOR.MINOR bump cuts a
Nerdbank.GitVersioning counts height from the commit that last changed
`version`, and that commit is itself height 1 -- so the first release of every
new MAJOR.MINOR landed as .1 and no .0 has ever existed here. 22 released
versions, zero ending in .0. Shipping `5.0.1` as the first 5.0 implies a 5.0.0
that was superseded, which never existed.
This MUST be introduced alongside a MAJOR.MINOR bump. Adding it mid-stream
shifts the next resolved version DOWN by one, which can land below what is
already on the feed -- exactly the trap CS2OpenDev.Sdk.GameEvents' positive
offset was created to escape, in the other direction.
Cannot make height negative in practice: the offset only applies from the
commit that sets it, which is a `version` change, so height is at least 1.
